source.title: HHS: Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule

stem: Under OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, what must an employer with occupational exposure put in place?
choices: A written exposure control plan
A sign at each sink reminding staff to wash hands
Annual HIV and hepatitis testing of every patient
A written ban on handling tears or lenses by hand
explanation: The standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) requires an exposure control plan describing engineering and work practice controls, personal protective equipment, training, medical surveillance, and hepatitis B vaccinations.

source.title: OSHA: Bloodborne Pathogens — Overview

stem: What does a higher modulus of elasticity mean clinically for a soft lens?
choices: Higher oxygen transmissibility at the same thickness
Fewer deposits and less papillary conjunctivitis
Better draping and less edge fluting on steep corneas
Easier handling, but more mechanical complications
explanation: Modulus describes resistance to deformation. Stiffer lenses handle better and are easier to check for inversion, but they are linked to CLPC, SEALs, limbal epithelial hypertrophy, mucin balls, and edge standoff.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Modulus and Its Effect on Contact Lens Fit, Feb 2007

stem: Why do many silicone hydrogel lenses need surface modification or wetting agents?
choices: Silicone makes the surface hydrophobic
Silicone blocks oxygen at the surface
Silicone makes the lens too soft to handle
Silicone reacts chemically with saline
explanation: Silicone hydrogels are slightly stiffer and their surface can be hydrophobic, which affects comfort. Manufacturers address this with surface treatments or wetting agents.

source.title: Wikipedia: Contact lens

stem: How did first- and second-generation silicone hydrogels improve surface wettability?
choices: 1st: plasma surface treatment; 2nd: internal wetting agents
1st: internal wetting agents; 2nd: plasma surface treatment
Both generations used thimerosal-based surface coatings
Both generations relied only on higher water content
explanation: First-generation silicone hydrogels used plasma coating to change the hydrophobic surface, second-generation lenses incorporated internal rewetting agents, and third-generation materials are inherently wettable without added treatments.

source.title: Wikipedia: Contact lens

stem: What is the basic construction of a modern hybrid contact lens?
choices: A soft center with a rigid outer ring
A rigid center with a soft skirt
A soft lens worn under a rigid lens
A scleral lens with a soft optic zone
explanation: Hybrids combine a rigid center for optics with a soft skirt for comfort. The skirt keeps the rigid center centered and limits movement, giving stable vision.

source.title: Optometric Management: Combining Vision and Comfort With Hybrid Lenses, Mar 2014

stem: Which patient is a good candidate for a hybrid lens designed for regular astigmatism?
choices: A patient who needs 30-night continuous wear
An astigmat who cannot tolerate GP comfort
A severe dry eye patient needing a fluid reservoir
A child who needs overnight myopia control
explanation: Hybrids suit patients with astigmatism or asymmetric corneas who need rigid optics but cannot wear GP lenses comfortably. Designs for regular astigmatism are not indicated for keratoconic or post-surgical corneas.

source.title: Optometric Management: Combining Vision and Comfort With Hybrid Lenses, Mar 2014

stem: How is a reverse-geometry hybrid such as UltraHealth fit for keratoconus?
choices: By choosing a base curve 0.1 mm flatter than flat K
By vault over the cornea, not by matching K readings
By selecting the skirt curve alone, ignoring the center
By three-point touch with bearing on the cone apex
explanation: Like a scleral lens, this design is fit by vault or elevation. The fitting guide expects the lens to settle 30–60 µm with wear, so vault is chosen to leave clearance over the apex after settling.

source.title: SynergEyes UltraHealth Fitting Guide (Rev E)

stem: What does overnight orthokeratology do?
choices: Permanently flattens the cornea after a few months of wear
Temporarily reshapes the cornea, mainly to reduce myopia
Uses soft lenses at night to reshape the crystalline lens
Permanently steepens the cornea to correct presbyopia
explanation: Ortho-K lenses are worn while sleeping and removed on waking. The effect is temporary; if lens wear stops, the cornea returns to its original curvature and myopia.

source.title: FDA: Types of Contact Lenses

stem: What does the FDA require of eye care professionals before fitting overnight ortho-K lenses?
choices: A separate state optician license
Patient enrollment in a clinical trial
No special training or requirements
Training and certification
explanation: The FDA requires eye care professionals to be trained and certified before using overnight ortho-K lenses in practice, and patients may ask which lenses their practitioner is certified to fit.

source.title: FDA: Types of Contact Lenses

stem: What safety lapse is most often behind serious ortho-K complications such as Acanthamoeba infection?
choices: Wearing the lenses only overnight as prescribed
Using a lens material with too high a Dk value
Poor hygiene, such as rinsing lenses in tap water
Removing the lenses promptly upon waking up
explanation: Complications typically come from failing to follow hygiene recommendations. Reported Acanthamoeba infections during ortho-K were possibly related to rinsing lenses in tap water.

source.title: Wikipedia: Orthokeratology

stem: What distinguishes a scleral lens from a corneal rigid lens?
choices: It rests on the central cornea with apical touch
It is a soft lens bonded to a rigid outer edge
It lands on the sclera and vaults the cornea
It is designed to be worn only during sleep
explanation: A scleral lens is large and rests on the sclera, creating a tear-filled vault over the cornea. The fluid layer masks corneal irregularity and protects the ocular surface.

source.title: Wikipedia: Scleral lens

stem: Which condition is a common indication for scleral lenses?
choices: Low myopia with a healthy cornea
A patient wanting overnight wear
Mild presbyopia only
Severe dry eye or ocular surface disease
explanation: Indications include severe dry eye, keratoconus and other ectasias, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, Sjögren's disease, neurotrophic keratitis, and complications after LASIK or corneal transplant.

source.title: Wikipedia: Scleral lens

stem: What are the three main principles of scleral lens fitting?
choices: Touch the corneal apex, move 1–2 mm, and ride slightly high
Match flat K, use a thin edge, and attach under the lid
Clear the cornea and limbus, land evenly, keep tear exchange
Rest on the limbus, avoid the sclera, and fit loosely
explanation: Scleral fitting aims to clear the cornea and limbus, land on the sclera with an even haptic, and keep adequate tear exchange. Vault depends more on total sagittal height than on base curve.

source.title: Review of Cornea & Contact Lenses: AS-OCT and the Specialty Contact Lens

stem: For an interpalpebral RGP fit, what axial edge lift and edge thickness are generally recommended?
choices: AEL about 80–110 µm; edge 0.09–0.12 mm
AEL about 300–400 µm; edge 0.20 mm
AEL of zero; a knife-sharp edge
AEL about 10–20 µm; edge 0.05 mm
explanation: AEL of 80–110 µm usually gives adequate tear exchange without excess lid interaction. Edges thinner than this tend to be sharp and chip, while lid-attachment designs use flatter peripheries and thicker edges.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Do Peripheral Curves Matter?, May 1997

stem: Using the rule of thumb for a tricurve RGP (secondary curve = base curve + 1.0 to 1.5 mm), which secondary curve fits a 7.80 mm base curve?
explanation: 7.80 + 1.0 = 8.80 mm and 7.80 + 1.5 = 9.30 mm, so 9.00 mm falls in range. The tertiary curve would then be the secondary radius plus 1.5 to 2.0 mm.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Do Peripheral Curves Matter?, May 1997

stem: What can happen if an RGP peripheral curve system is too steep?
choices: Excess lens movement and a wide lid gap at the edge
Inferior decentration from an overly flat periphery
Lens binding, poor tear exchange, and chafing
Improved oxygen supply and fresher limbal tears
explanation: A periphery that is too steep traps the lens with poor tear exchange and chafes the peripheral cornea. Too flat a periphery creates lid gap or inferior decentration, both associated with 3 and 9 o'clock staining.

source.title: Contact Lens Spectrum: Do Peripheral Curves Matter?, May 1997
